summary: Describes two fully specified forward erasure correction schemes using sliding window random linear codes, one over GF(2) and one over GF(2^8), with controllable code density. They protect media streams under the extended FECFRAME framework and cut latency compared to block codes.

eli5.summary: The sender mixes pieces of the message into extra pieces. If some pieces are lost on the way, the receiver can solve a puzzle to recover them.

questions: what is sliding window rlc fec

subtitle: Two ways to protect live media streams from packet loss by sending random mixtures of recent packets as repair data.

tldr.problem: Block-based forward erasure correction codes make every receiver wait for a whole block, which adds delay for real-time media sent to many receivers with different loss rates.
tldr.mechanism: A window slides over the source symbols, and each repair symbol is a random linear combination of the symbols in the window, over either GF(2) or GF(2^8), with a density threshold that controls how many coefficients are nonzero.
tldr.outcome: Receivers with good links recover an isolated loss quickly from the next repair packet, and the scheme is registered as FEC Encoding IDs 9 (GF(2)) and 10 (GF(2^8)) for FECFRAME.

today: RFC 8681 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the sliding window extension in RFC 8680.

sections.title: What the Document Defines
sections.content:
RFC 8681 specifies two fully specified Forward Erasure Correction (FEC) schemes for FECFRAME, the framework of RFC 6363 that protects continuous media against packet loss. Both are Sliding Window Random Linear Codes (RLC): one works over the Galois Field GF(2) and the other over GF(2^8). Each lets the sender control the code density.

The document is aimed at multicast and broadcast delivery of content with strict real-time constraints, where each source packet has a maximum validity period after which the destination application will not use it. It applies the FECFRAME extension to sliding window codes from RFC 8680.
sections.eli5: This document describes two recipes for adding backup pieces to a live video or audio stream. If some pieces are lost, the backups let the receiver rebuild them in time.

sections.title: Why Block Codes Hurt Real-Time Flows
sections.content:
The FEC codes already standardized for FECFRAME (Reed-Solomon, LDPC-Staircase and Raptor/RaptorQ) are all linear block codes: the data flow must be cut into blocks of a predefined maximum size. A larger block gives more robustness against long bursts of loss, but also a higher maximum decoding latency. Because no encoding can happen until all the source data of a block is available, the block size set for the worst receiver also delays receivers with good connections.

A sliding window code avoids this. Repair symbols are generated on the fly as random linear combinations of the source symbols currently in the encoding window. An isolated lost source packet is recovered with the following repair packet, whereas with a block code the receiver always has to wait for the first repair packet after the end of the block. The RFC adds that, in some situations, a sliding window code can reach a target quality with fewer repair packets.
sections.eli5: A block code is like a teacher who only hands out the answer key after the whole test is finished. A sliding window code hands out a hint right after each question, so you do not wait.

sections.title: Parameters, ADUIs and the Encoding Window
sections.content:
The codec relies on a few parameters: the maximum FEC-related latency budget max_lat, the symbol size E in bytes, the code rate cr (source symbols over source plus repair symbols), the encoding window current and maximum sizes ew_size and ew_max_size, and at the receiver the decoding window and linear system maximum sizes dw_max_size and ls_max_size. The sender MUST fix E and communicate it, and ls_max_size SHOULD NOT be smaller than dw_max_size.

Application data units (ADUs) are not mapped directly to symbols. For each ADU the sender builds an ADUI by prepending a 1-byte Flow ID (F) and a 2-byte Length (L), then adding zero padding so the total is a multiple of E. The three prepended bytes and the padding are not sent on the network but are protected by the code, so a receiver that recovers an ADUI can drop the padding and find the right flow.

Each source symbol has an Encoding Symbol ID (ESI) that starts at 0 and increases sequentially. When the window reaches ew_max_size, the oldest symbol MUST be removed before a new one is added. Symbols of an expired ADU SHOULD also be removed.
sections.eli5: Before sending, each message gets a small label saying which stream it belongs to and how long it is, and is padded to fit whole boxes. The sender only keeps the newest boxes in its mixing bowl and throws out the oldest ones.

sections.title: Coefficients, PRNG and Finite Fields
sections.content:
The coding coefficients are produced by the generate_coding_coefficients() function from a repair key (the seed) and a Density Threshold DT between 0 and 15. The average probability of a nonzero coefficient is (DT + 1) / 16, and with DT equal to 15 all coefficients are nonzero. The random numbers come from the TinyMT32 generator of RFC 8682, reduced to 4 or 8 bits by masking with 0xF or 0xFF. Any implementation MUST produce the same output as the reference, and Appendix A gives validation values for seed 1.

Field arithmetic reuses the fields of RFC 5510. Addition is a bitwise XOR. In GF(2^8), multiplication is modulo the irreducible polynomial x^8 + x^4 + x^3 + x^2 + 1. In GF(2), multiplication is a logical AND, so a repair symbol is simply the XOR of the source symbols whose coefficient is 1. With GF(2^8) each byte of the repair symbol is the XOR of coefficient-times-source-byte terms over the whole window.
sections.eli5: Sender and receiver share the same dice-rolling recipe. Because both start from the same number, they roll the same dice and agree on how the pieces were mixed, without the sender listing every ingredient.

sections.title: Payload IDs and Registered Encoding IDs
sections.content:
Each FEC Source Packet carries a 32-bit Explicit Source FEC Payload ID appended at its end, holding the ESI of the first source symbol of its ADUI. Each FEC Repair Packet carries a 64-bit Repair FEC Payload ID prepended to the repair symbol. It holds a 16-bit Repair_Key, the 4-bit DT, a 12-bit NSS (number of source symbols in the window) and a 32-bit FSS_ESI (ESI of the first source symbol in the window). From these the receiver rebuilds the exact window and coefficients without a list of symbols. A repair packet MAY hold several repair symbols, found by dividing the packet size by E; their repair keys are the first key plus 1, 2 and so on.

The session configuration (FFCI, for example in SDP) carries the Encoding ID plus E and a Window Size Ratio (WSR, 0 to 255). Encoding ID 10 is the GF(2^8) scheme and 9 is the GF(2) scheme; IANA registers both. In the GF(2) scheme, when DT is 15 the Repair_Key is useless, so the sender MUST set it to zero and a receiver MUST ignore it.
sections.eli5: Each backup piece has a small tag with the few numbers a receiver needs: which pieces were mixed and which dice seed was used. Every piece is tagged the same way, however many pieces were mixed.

sections.title: How the Encoder and Decoder Work
sections.content:
To make a repair packet, the encoder gathers the ew_size symbols in the window, picks a repair key (for example a counter that wraps to 0 after 65535), generates that many coefficients, and computes the linear combination. The choice of repair key is entirely up to the sender, and a receiver should not assume anything about how it is managed.

The decoder keeps a linear system whose variables are the received and lost source symbols. Each repair packet that covers at least one lost symbol adds an equation, built with the same coefficient function from the repair key and window description. When a sub-system covering lost symbols is of full rank, those symbols are recovered; Gaussian elimination is one possible method. Recovered ADUIs are stripped of padding and handed to the right flow. Whether a late ADU is discarded, and when received packets are passed up, is an operational decision left to the application.
sections.eli5: Every backup piece is one clue about the lost pieces. When the receiver has enough clues, it solves the puzzle, finds the missing piece and puts it back in the right stream.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The scheme mostly inherits the recommendations of RFC 6363: use confidentiality and integrity protection for the data flow, and IPsec/ESP is mandatory to implement but not mandatory to use. The RFC lists what an attacker can do by changing parameters. Altering the Encoding ID or E in the session configuration causes denial of service or corrupted content. Altering the ESI, Repair_Key, DT, NSS or FSS_ESI makes a receiver use wrong symbols or coefficients, so decoded data is corrupted. Raising DT or NSS also raises processing load at the receiver.

It is RECOMMENDED to protect the integrity of the session configuration and of both source and repair packets. Because the document adds formulae, it also RECOMMENDS checking that computed values and any RTP timestamps used stay within reasonable bounds, to avoid overflows.
sections.eli5: If a bad person scribbles on the tags, the receiver mixes the wrong pieces and gets garbage. So the tags and settings need a lock that shows nobody changed them.

sections.title: Choosing the Field and the Density
sections.content:
The RFC expects the GF(2^8) scheme to be the most used because it gives higher loss protection. For small windows its processing cost is not an issue: the authors report measured decoding speeds between 745 Mbps and 2.8 Gbps on an ARM Cortex-A15 board, with windows of 18 or 23 symbols. The GF(2) scheme is an alternative where symbols are directly XOR-ed, which is fast and can suit large windows, but protection is significantly reduced.

For density, small windows with GF(2^8) usually suit DT equal to 15. Larger windows usually call for a lower value, or GF(2) with DT of 7 (an average density of 1/2) or smaller. Using DT 15 with GF(2) is equivalent to an XOR code over the whole window, so only a single repair symbol can be produced for any window.
sections.eli5: One recipe is stronger but takes more brain work; the other is quicker but catches fewer mistakes. You pick based on how big your mixing bowl is.
